node.label: Paige Raibmon
node.date_label: Authentic Indians (2005) · Unmaking Native Space (2008) · Written as I Remember It (2014) · As I Remember It (2019)
node.description: Paige Raibmon argues that colonial definitions of Indigenous authenticity shaped access to land, resources and sovereignty. Authentic Indians (2005) traces how Indigenous people negotiated these imposed categories in Northwest Coast encounters, joining cultural and labour history. Brian W. Dippie’s 2006 review welcomed the book’s contribution but questioned whether its opposing categories oversimplified civilization and obscured the racial basis of exclusion. In “Unmaking Native Space” (2008), Raibmon connects official land policy to everyday settler practices, using a genealogical method drawn from Foucault to show how dispossession emerged from contingent interactions rather than policy alone. Her later collaborations make the research relationship and the form of publication part of historical method: Written as I Remember It (2014) credits Elsie Paul with Raibmon and Harmony Johnson; As I Remember It (2019) is a separate multimedia publication with additional collaborators. Her essay on transformational listening asks listeners to examine their assumptions rather than assume that hearing testimony automatically transforms colonial relationships.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Authentic Indians: Episodes of Encounter from the Late-Nineteenth-Century Northwest Coast (2005); “Unmaking Native Space” (2008); Written as I Remember It (2014), by Elsie Paul with Paige Raibmon and Harmony Johnson; As I Remember It (2019), by Elsie Paul with Davis McKenzie and Paige Raibmon, with contributions by Harmony Johnson and Honoré Watanabe.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Unmaking Native Space” (2008), Raibmon credits Harris’s Making Native Space (2002) but criticizes its transfer of metropolitan rhetoric onto settler society without sufficiently distinguishing rhetoric from practice.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Author-posted chapter, p. 58 and note 74, pp. 84–85: “conflation of rhetoric and practice.” Qualified criticism; she credits Harris with implicating settlers. Harris’s book not freshly read; no general rejection of it asserted.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Unmaking Native Space” (2008), Raibmon explicitly adopts Foucault’s genealogical method to trace contingent connections between settler practices and dispossession.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Printed pp. 58–59, 76 and notes 7–9, 71 (pp. 80, 84). Her term “genealogical” is developed through Foucault’s “Nietzsche, Genealogy, History,” cited in the 1984 Foucault Reader. That edition is the witness she used; Foucault’s essay not independently read in this research.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Transformational Listening” (2019 review version), Raibmon draws explicitly on Cruikshank’s warning about comparing another person’s life account with one’s own to explain the limits of sympathetic listening.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher review version, section “Resisting False Equivalency,” paragraph beginning “Unless we resist this pull”: names Cruikshank and warns against “implicit comparisons.” Cruikshank’s underlying text not identified here or freshly read; final 2019 chapter not collated. No shared-employer inference.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Provincializing Europe in Canadian History” (2018), Raibmon explicitly borrows the title and terminology of Chakrabarty’s Provincializing Europe (2000) to challenge supposedly universal European categories in history teaching.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Opening definition of provincializing and note 1: “I borrow terminology here.” Editor’s note also identifies the reference. This establishes the stated conceptual debt; Chakrabarty’s book is not freshly read and no personal mentorship is inferred.

proposed_edges.relationship: Reviewing Authentic Indians (2005) in 2006, Michael E. Harkin compares it with Deloria’s Playing Indian (1998), distinguishing Indigenous negotiations of identity from Euro-American performances of Indianness.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Journal of American History 93:1 (2006), p. 236, displayed extract, paragraph beginning “Rather, ethnicity”: Harkin calls it “in a sense” a response. Undirected, explicitly a reviewer’s comparison; neither direct debt nor exchange is established. Full review and both books unread in full.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Unmaking Native Space” (2008), Raibmon uses Perry’s On the Edge of Empire (2001) to argue that evidence of individual relationships must remain connected to colonial power and that consequential practices need not share intentions.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Printed p. 75, two paragraphs beginning “And what of” and “Such genealogical connections,” with notes 69–70 on p. 84 citing Perry pp. 62, 75. Short phrase “bound by chronology.” Methodological use only; no genealogy or account of individual families reproduced. Perry’s book not freshly read.

proposed_edges.relationship: Authentic Indians (2005) explains how colonial definitions of authenticity constrained Indigenous claims to land, resources and sovereignty while Indigenous actors negotiated those definitions.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Duke publisher description, paragraphs beginning “In this innovative history” and “They recognized.” Publisher summary only; book not read in full. Existing native_newcomer roster row and bodies_missions_authenticity strand already name the work; this person-to-field edge is additive, not a duplicate roster proposal. No existing edge incident on paige_raibmon.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “The Practice of Everyday Colonialism” (2006), Raibmon criticizes labour history’s separation of Indigenous culture from modern wage work and calls for rethinking its analytical categories.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Printed pp. 23, 25–26 and 56, author-posted article: rejects the binary of “traditional culture” and “modern labor.” Field-level historiographical criticism explicitly addressed to labour historians; claim does not reproduce community knowledge. Middle of article unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Transformational Listening” (2019 review version), Raibmon argues that hearing testimony requires sustained self-questioning and does not by itself guarantee reconciliation or decolonization.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Sections “Stories Are a Gift” and “Resisting False Equivalency,” plus final two paragraphs; term “transformational listening.” This is Raibmon’s methodological argument in the identified publisher review text, not a claim to authorship of collaborators’ knowledge. Final chapter not collated.

proposed_edges.relationship: Written as I Remember It (2014), by Elsie Paul with Raibmon and Harmony Johnson, and the separate digital As I Remember It (2019) make collaborative authorship and publication form part of historical practice.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: UBC Press authorship credits and collaborative-research description for the 2014 book; separate digital-book credits; Raibmon’s UBC Research section. Scholarship and production process only. Lead authorship remains Paul’s, and the two publications retain distinct collaborator credits. Full books unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In ‘Unmaking Native Space’ (2008), Paige Raibmon contributes a genealogical approach to histories of settler colonialism that brings settlement and Indigenous dispossession into the same analysis, as Daniel Rück explains in The Laws and the Land (2021).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the publisher’s introduction excerpt, especially p. 7. Rück attributes this approach to Raibmon by name and explicitly positions his own book within that discussion. This supplies a substantive later assessment of her contribution to studying settler colonies. The edge records that methodological contribution, not the detailed historical contents of Rück’s case study. Raibmon’s UBC bibliography confirms the chapter’s original publication in The Power of Promises (2008). No new reading of the 2008 chapter is claimed. Rück has no endpoint in either supplied roster, so no person-to-person edge to him is proposed.

proposed_edges.relationship: In ‘Obvious but Invisible: Ways of Knowing Health, Environment, and Colonialism in a West Coast Indigenous Community’ (2018), Paige Raibmon contributes to environmental history by examining how state standards of evidence and assessments of risk shape the recognition of pollution claims under settler colonialism.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read Raibmon’s analytical opening, pp. 241–245, in her own article posted by her university and linked from her research bibliography. The opening connects scientific authorization, state risk calculations, environmental justice and colonial recognition; pp. 242–243 specify why struggles on Indigenous lands require a distinct analysis. The environmental-history classification is editorial and rests on this explicit argument, not on a declared research interest. Only the scholarly framework is recorded: no narrator quotations, oral narratives, teachings, genealogies or community knowledge are reproduced. No claim to have read the entire article is made. The DOI request did not resolve through the reading tool; the author’s institutional copy supplied the passage.

row.context: Develops transformational listening as a self-questioning practice for audiences of testimony.
Criticizes the exclusion of Indigenous workers from labour history’s categories and links wage work to colonial representation.
Collaborative historical publications foreground process and form while preserving Elsie Paul’s lead authorship.
